pages.name: Stretch
pages.text: This is the square from lesson 3, `y = x²`. Pull the top handle and every output is multiplied by its number, so at 2 all four height arrows double at once. That is `2f(x)`, a [[vertical stretch]], and the bottom stays at `(0, 0)` because 2 × 0 is 0.
pages.alt: A graph of y equals 2f(x) equals 2x squared, input along the bottom and output up the side. A dashed copy shows where it started. Arrows from the x-axis show the heights of 4 marked points. A label reads 8. A label reads 2. A label reads 2. A label reads 8.

pages.name: Three times as tall
pages.task: `y = √x` passes through `(4, 2)`. Where is that point on `y = 3√x`?
pages.why: `3√x` puts 4 through the root to get 2, then multiplies by 3, giving 6. The input stays 4, so `(4, 2)` rises straight up to `(4, 6)`, and its height arrow is three times as long.

pages.name: Squash and flip
pages.text: Below 1 the top handle squashes the graph, so at ½ the point `(2, 4)` drops to `(2, 2)`. At 0 the graph lies flat on the `x`-axis, and on through it to −1 every height changes sign. That is `−f(x)`, the graph flipped over the `x`-axis, a [[reflection]].
pages.alt: A graph of y equals minus f(x) equals minus x squared, input along the bottom and output up the side. A dashed copy shows where it started. Arrows from the x-axis show the heights of 4 marked points. A label reads minus 4. A label reads minus 1. A label reads minus 1. A label reads minus 4.

pages.name: Flip the root
pages.task: `y = √x` passes through `(9, 3)`. Where is that point on `y = −√x`?
pages.why: `−√x` puts 9 through the root to get 3, then changes its sign, giving −3. The input stays 9, so `(9, 3)` flips straight down to `(9, −3)`, over the `x`-axis.

pages.name: Squeeze
pages.text: Now the square root, drawn from 0 to 9. The side handle doubles every input before the machine, so an input half as big gives the old output, and every point moves halfway in towards the `y`-axis. That is `f(2x)`, the graph squeezed sideways.
pages.alt: A graph of y equals f(2x) equals the square root of (2x), input along the bottom and output up the side. A dashed copy shows where it started. Arrows from the y-axis show the inputs of 3 marked points. A label reads 0.5. A label reads 2. A label reads 4.5.

pages.name: Three inside
pages.why: `√(3x)` gives 3 when `3x` is 9, which is at `x = 3`. Check it. `√(3 × 3) = √9 = 3`. Each input need only be a third as big, so `(9, 3)` moves in to `(3, 3)`.

pages.name: Through the y-axis
pages.text: Pull the side handle on through the `y`-axis: the graph squeezes right in to the axis and out the other side, and every input changes sign. That is `f(−x) = √(−x)`, which takes only inputs of 0 and below, so `(4, 2)` moves to `(−4, 2)`. A minus inside flips the graph over the `y`-axis.
pages.alt: A graph of y equals f( minus x) equals the square root of ( minus x), input along the bottom and output up the side. A dashed copy shows where it started. Arrows from the y-axis show the inputs of 3 marked points. A label reads minus 1. A label reads minus 4. A label reads minus 9.

pages.name: Which flip?
pages.task: This is `y = √x` flipped, so `(9, 3)` now sits at `(−9, 3)`. Which rule is it?
pages.why: The point moved from `x = 9` to `x = −9`, so every input has changed sign, and the minus goes inside. Check one point. `√(−(−4)) = √4 = 2`, so `√(−x)` passes through `(−4, 2)`.

pages.name: The transmitter
pages.text: The transmitter from lesson 2 starts from the fraction of full scale, `p ÷ 100`, which runs from 0 to 1 and has no unit. The top handle stretches it by the [[gain]], 16 mA for full scale, so it runs from 0 to 16 mA, and lesson 5's slide lifts it 4 mA, the [[offset]], so it runs from 4 to 20 mA. At 50% that gives 0.5, then 8 mA, then 12 mA.
pages.alt: A graph of S(p) equals 16f(p) plus 4 equals 0.16p plus 4, input along the bottom and output up the side. A dashed copy shows where it started. Arrows from the x-axis show the heights of 1 marked point. A label reads (50 percent, 0.5) goes to (50 percent, 12 mA). A label reads gain times 16. A label reads offset 4 mA.

pages.name: Flip, then lift
pages.task: `y = x²` passes through `(2, 4)`. How high is `y = −x² + 2` at `x = 2`?
pages.why: `−x² + 2` squares 2 to get 4, flips it to −4, then adds 2, giving −2. So `(2, 4)` flips down to `(2, −4)` and is then lifted to `(2, −2)`.

pages.name: Inside and out
pages.task: Where does the point `(2, 4)` of `y = x²` go on `y = −(2x)²`?
pages.why: Inside, `2x` halves every input, so `(2, 4)` moves in to `(1, 4)`. Outside, the minus flips the height, so it lands on `(1, −4)`. Check it. `−(2 × 1)² = −4`.

pages.name: A faulty gain
pages.task: A transmitter's gain has been set to 8 instead of 16, with its offset still 4 mA. What does it send at 50%?
pages.why: At 50% the fraction is 0.5. The gain of 8 stretches it to 8 × 0.5 = 4 mA, and the offset lifts it 4 mA, so it sends 8 mA instead of 12 mA. The line is half as steep and still starts at 4 mA.

pages.name: Looking ahead
pages.text: One look ahead, at an AC wave sketched here with a peak of 1. The top handle stretches it to a peak of 2, a DC offset lifts it by 1 so it runs from −1 to 3, and a slide to the right is a delay. Its own rule waits for the Trigonometry course.
pages.alt: A graph of stretched times 2, lifted 1, delayed, input along the bottom and output up the side. A dashed copy shows where it started. Arrows from the x-axis show the heights of 2 marked points. A label reads 3. A label reads minus 1.
